task.goal: Teach new sewing volunteers to notice when seam allowance changes the finished size of a simple fabric pouch.
hard_constraints: Use scrap fabric and existing hand tools; no cutting of donated finished garments.
Do not require machine sewing or assume the same hand dexterity for every learner.
In 40 minutes, compare a prediction with a measured paper or fabric prototype and allow a non-sewing participation path.
task.available_resources: Scraps, paper templates, rulers, clips, needles and thread.
task.expected_result: A practical lesson that tests size reasoning and accommodates different abilities.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Same template, different seam lines
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Use a controlled comparison: identical panels produce different finished widths when the stitch lines move inward. Prepare two pairs of 16 × 14 cm paper panels, representing a pouch sewn along both sides and the bottom, with an open top. Mark seam lines 1 cm from the edges on one pair and 2 cm on the other. Before assembling, learners predict each pouch’s flat width and height using words, numbers, or pointing to ruler marks. Clip panels together, fold allowances back at the marked lines, and measure between the side seam lines and from the bottom seam line to the top: expected dimensions are 14 × 13 cm and 12 × 12 cm. Explain that width loses allowance twice, while height loses it once in this open-top design.

Spend 5 minutes introducing the pouch, 7 predicting, 13 assembling, 10 measuring and comparing, and 5 applying the idea to a fresh example. Paper is a complete non-sewing route; volunteers may instead hand-stitch scrap pairs. Offer predictor, clip placer, measurer, and recorder roles, with assistance by choice. No donated garments are cut. This assumes a flat, unhemmed pouch with straight seams; usable interior capacity and fabric thickness are separate questions.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Use the 1 cm pouch as the comparator for the 2 cm pouch. Record predictions before revealing measurements. The mechanism predicts that increasing allowance by 1 cm reduces width by 2 cm and height by 1 cm. If measurements disagree, inspect seam placement and measurement endpoints. Finally ask learners to predict dimensions for a 1.5 cm allowance on the same template; check against a folded paper prototype. Correct assembly without a correct new prediction suggests the size reasoning needs another example.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Work backward from an object that must fit
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Make seam allowance matter through a fit requirement. Learners create a 10 cm-wide paper gauge representing an object, then design a flat, open-top pouch with at least 11 cm between its side seam lines. With a 1 cm allowance on each side, the paper panels must be at least 13 cm wide. Compare this with an intuitive baseline: panels only 11 cm wide. Learners predict whether each design will meet the requirement before clipping paired paper panels and folding back their side allowances. Measure the clear flat width and try placing the gauge between the seam lines without bending it.

Allocate 5 minutes to the brief, 8 to predictions and template selection, 12 to assembly, 10 to measurement and fit checks, and 5 to redesign. Use paper, rulers, and clips throughout; optional hand stitching on scraps can demonstrate the same boundary. A partner can draw or manipulate materials while a learner chooses dimensions, checks arithmetic, or reports fit. No sewing is necessary for completion.

The primary mechanism is backward planning: desired finished size determines panel size after accounting for both seams. It assumes a thin, flat gauge, straight seams, and no lining or top hem. Real bulky objects need additional ease, so success here establishes the width rule rather than guaranteeing a practical carrying pouch.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Compare the 11 cm-wide baseline panels with the calculated 13 cm-wide panels, keeping allowance at 1 cm. Their predicted finished widths are 9 cm and 11 cm. Measure before testing the gauge so fit does not replace numerical evidence. A small transfer check changes the allowance to 2 cm: ask learners to select a panel width that preserves the 11 cm target, then inspect a paper prototype. Choosing 15 cm supports backward reasoning; choosing 13 cm again reveals that the seam change was not incorporated.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Find why the pouch became narrower
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Teach through diagnosis and repair. Present two clipped paper pouch prototypes made from equal 16 cm-wide panels. One has side seam lines 1 cm from both edges; the other has lines 1 cm from one edge and 3 cm from the other. Leave tops open and use the same bottom allowance. Ask learners to predict which pouch is narrower and by how much, then measure widths between side seam lines. The expected widths are 14 cm and 12 cm. Learners inspect the unequal margins and identify which boundary caused the change.

Next, ask them to restore the narrower prototype to 14 cm without changing its panel width. They can move the 3 cm seam line to 1 cm, refold, and reclip; optional scrap stitching may follow. This makes seam placement an adjustable cause rather than treating allowance as a memorized formula. It also shows that the two side allowances add even when unequal.

Use 5 minutes for the problem, 7 for prediction, 10 for inspection and measurement, 10 for repair, and 8 for explanation and a new case. Paper prototypes, rulers, and clips suffice. Learners may direct a partner, compare marks visually, record results, or explain the repair without handling needles. It assumes seam lines can be represented accurately by folds; paper stiffness and clip placement may introduce measurement error. Use only paper or scraps, with no cutting of donated garments.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Keep the symmetric 1 cm prototype unchanged as the comparator. Record the narrower pouch’s predicted width, measured width, proposed repair, and post-repair width. Moving just the misplaced seam should recover about 2 cm. If it does not, inspect folds and panel alignment. For a transfer check, show a 16 cm panel with 2 cm and 3 cm side allowances; ask for its finished width before making the folds. An 11 cm prediction supports understanding that both margins contribute, rather than simply doubling one allowance.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Does this edge consume seam allowance?
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Teach learners to distinguish a folded boundary from a sewn boundary before calculating size. The mechanism is construction awareness: allowance reduces a dimension where a seam sits inside a cut edge; a bottom fold does not consume a bottom seam allowance.

Use existing paper templates: one 16 × 28 cm sheet folded into a 16 × 14 cm pouch outline, and two separate 16 × 14 cm panels. Both designs have an open, unhemmed top and side seam lines 1 cm inward. The separate panels also need a bottom seam, initially 1 cm inward. Learners predict each finished flat height, then predict what happens if the bottom seam allowance becomes 2 cm. They may speak, point to ruler marks, or direct a partner.

Allocate 6 minutes to inspecting the constructions, 7 to predictions, 12 to folding and clipping, 10 to measurement and comparison, and 5 to a fresh prediction. Clip the paper models, fold seam margins outward, and measure from the top edge to the bottom boundary. The folded model should remain 14 cm high; the separate-panel model should change from 13 to 12 cm. Both have 14 cm between side seam lines.

Paper, rulers, and clips suffice. Optional scrap examples can illustrate the same construction without requiring sewing. Learners can choose predictor, measurer, recorder, or partner-director roles; no donated garments are cut. This assumes suitable existing templates, straight boundaries, and flat measurements. Paper models establish geometric size, not usable capacity, and fold thickness may cause small measurement differences.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Record predictions before assembly. Keep the folded-bottom model as the comparator while moving only the separate-panel model’s bottom seam from 1 to 2 cm. A 1 cm height reduction in the latter, with no change in the former, supports the construction rule. If both shrink, inspect whether someone mistakenly folded an allowance into the folded bottom. For transfer, ask learners to predict the separate-panel height with a 3 cm bottom allowance and identify whether that allowance applies to the folded model. Check their predictions against the paper models; applying the deduction to both reveals that the distinction needs reteaching.

DIRECT_FULL.title: A pouch can be wide at the opening and narrow in the middle
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Teach through a measurement trap: checking only the opening can hide size lost to an inward-wandering seam. What changes the outcome is the largest local seam allowance, so learners investigate width along the pouch rather than treating finished width as one uniform number.

Use two pairs of existing 16 × 14 cm paper templates representing flat, open-top pouches. On the first, mark both side seam lines 1 cm from the edges. On the second, keep the left line at 1 cm; mark the right line at 1 cm near the top and bottom, curving inward to 3 cm at mid-height. Both have a 1 cm bottom allowance. An instructor can prepare the marks using a needle tip, or learners can indicate the boundaries with clips and ruler positions; no drawing tool is essential.

Spend 5 minutes inspecting the outlines, 7 predicting whether equal opening widths mean equal widths throughout, 12 aligning and clipping the paper prototypes, 11 measuring, and 5 explaining the result. Measure horizontally between seam lines near the opening and at mid-height. Expected widths are 14 cm throughout the straight model, versus 14 cm at the opening and 12 cm at the middle of the curved model.

Learners can predict verbally, point, read ruler marks, record findings, or direct a partner. Sewing is optional; suitable scraps can replace paper. No donated garments are cut. This assumes aligned panels and flat measurements. Paper demonstrates the size boundary; fabric stretch, thickness, and three-dimensional capacity remain outside the lesson.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Record predictions before measuring. Use the straight-seam prototype as the comparator and check both models at the same heights. The claim fails for the constructed models if the inward curve produces no local reduction after alignment and measurement endpoints are verified. Then show a fresh seam outline whose inward bulge occurs lower down: ask learners to identify and predict its narrowest width before measuring. Checking only the opening indicates that the central lesson needs another demonstration.

EXPAND.title: Reveal which edge becomes the finished boundary
EXPAND.proposal:
Teach boundary recognition through turning a pouch inside out. The facilitator prepares one loosely hand-stitched scrap pouch from two 16 × 14 cm panels, with 2 cm side and bottom allowances and an unfinished open top. Prepare a matching paper representation with allowances folded behind the face. Preparation requires only scraps, paper templates, rulers, needles, thread, and clips; never cut donated finished garments.

Use 5 minutes to introduce the pouch, 6 for predictions, 9 to turn and inspect it, 10 to measure and compare, and 10 for transfer. Before turning, learners predict its finished flat width and height and point to the boundaries they think will determine those measurements. Turn it right side out, measure it flat without stretching, then turn it back and trace how the raw edges sit inside the pouch. Expected dimensions are approximately 12 × 12 cm. The paper model provides straighter measurement boundaries if fabric wrinkles obscure the relationship.

The mechanism is making a hidden boundary visible: learners connect the seam line with the finished edge and see why the original cut edge cannot determine finished size. A facilitator or partner handles all turning and sewing; learners can predict verbally, point, direct measurement, or record results. Everyone completes the same reasoning task without needing to sew.

This assumes a flat pouch without lining, a top hem, or boxed corners. Thick fabric and loose stitching may affect measurements; use the paper model to distinguish geometry from construction variation.
EXPAND.experiment: The facilitator owns a first trial with two small groups: one uses the reveal sequence; the other uses the prior same-template, different-seam-lines lesson, with equal time. Both predict and identify measurement boundaries on an unfamiliar paper pouch before its dimensions are measured. Record correct predictions, boundary choices, and requests for handling assistance. Stop the reveal activity after 9 minutes if turning remains difficult and use its prepared paper model. Retain this route only if boundary recognition improves without reducing completed prediction checks; otherwise the extra preparation has not earned its place.

EXPAND.title: Explain a completed prototype, then withdraw the support
EXPAND.proposal:
Remove learner construction from the critical path and spend the time on interpreting finished examples. Before the lesson, the facilitator prepares three clipped paper pouch models with allowances folded behind their faces: two worked examples and one concealed transfer model. Use straight, open-top designs without a hem. Paper templates, rulers, and clips suffice; scrap fabric can illustrate the corresponding seam, but stitching is unnecessary.

Spend 5 minutes introducing the task, 8 examining a completed example, 7 explaining a partly worked example, 10 predicting and measuring the concealed model, and 10 discussing discrepancies and trying another prediction. The first example uses 16 × 14 cm panels with 1 cm allowances: show the measured 14 × 13 cm face and explain where each lost centimetre went. For the second, use the same panels with 2 cm allowances; provide only the width explanation and ask learners to explain the height. Finally, conceal the completed face of an 18 × 15 cm model with 2 cm allowances. Learners predict its dimensions before revealing and measuring it: 14 × 13 cm.

The mechanism is reducing construction demands while gradually removing explanatory support. This targets learners whose attention is consumed by aligning, folding, or manipulating materials before they can reason about size. Learners may answer through speech, pointing to ruler marks, or directing a partner; the facilitator supplies all physical manipulation if needed.

The essential prerequisite is accurate prepared models and explanations that connect each deduction to a physical boundary. Copying arithmetic remains a risk, so the final example changes both panel dimensions. This route establishes size reasoning, not independent pouch construction. No donated garments are used.
EXPAND.experiment: The facilitator compares this sequence with the prior learner-assembled, same-template comparison in one small trial, using equal 40-minute sessions. Both groups receive an unfamiliar paper prototype and predict its width and height before measurement. Record correct predictions with explanations, completed checks, facilitator preparation minutes, and assistance requests. Stop adding worked examples after minute 20 so every learner reaches an independent prediction. If completion increases but independent reasoning does not, or preparation substantially outweighs saved lesson time, prefer the simpler prior route.

EXPAND.title: Decide when nominal allowance is enough information
EXPAND.proposal:
Teach volunteers when they can predict size from a stated allowance and when they should request a measurement. Prepare clipped paper pouch prototypes with straight, parallel seam boundaries. Include two equal 16 cm-wide examples: one with verified 1 cm allowances on both sides, and another labelled 'about 1 cm' whose concealed allowances are actually 1.5 cm each. A third, unfamiliar example uses 18 cm panels with verified unequal allowances of 1 cm and 2 cm. Keep bottom allowances constant and focus assessment on finished flat width.

Use 5 minutes to establish the rule, 8 for the first two predictions and action choices, 10 to reveal and measure, 10 for the unfamiliar example, and 7 for discussion. The rule is: calculate when panel width and both side allowances are verified; otherwise give a conditional prediction and ask someone to measure the missing boundaries. Learners may choose 'calculate' or 'request measurement' verbally or by pointing. A partner performs any manipulation. Once measurements arrive, everyone completes a numerical prediction and compares it with the measured paper face.

The mechanism is controlling information quality before applying the size rule. The close pair yields widths of 14 cm and 13 cm, showing why an unverified nominal allowance can mislead. The unfamiliar example yields 15 cm and checks that unequal allowances do not themselves require a handoff when both are known.

The facilitator prepares and measures models using paper templates, rulers, and clips; optional scrap examples require no learner sewing. No donated garments are cut. This teaches a local decision rule for straight, flat pouches. Curved seams, thickness, hems, and usable capacity remain outside the calculation.
EXPAND.experiment: The facilitator compares this lesson with the prior asymmetric-seam diagnosis lesson. Give both groups the close pair and unfamiliar case, asking for an action choice and prediction before revealing measurements. Record correct calculate/request choices, final width accuracy, and unnecessary measurement requests. Stop each information search after one request: the facilitator supplies the missing measurement so reasoning can continue. Reject the added decision rule if it produces more checking without fewer unsupported predictions, or if learners routinely request help on the fully specified unfamiliar case.

EXPAND.title: Compare seam allowances with a bounded assembly recovery
EXPAND.proposal:
Upgrade source: “Same template, different seam lines.” Preserve its controlled comparison and add an assembly checkpoint with an immediate fallback, so inaccurate folds or unfinished stitching do not consume the prediction-and-measurement task.

The facilitator prepares paired 16 × 14 cm paper panels with side and bottom seam lines at either 1 cm or 2 cm. Keep tops open and unhemmed. Use 5 minutes to introduce the design, 7 to record individual predictions, 13 to assemble, 10 to measure and compare, and 5 for transfer. Expected flat dimensions are 14 × 13 cm and 12 × 12 cm: width loses two allowances, height one.

At minute 20, the facilitator checks whether both side boundaries and the bottom boundary remain visible and aligned with their marks. If any boundary is displaced by more than 2 mm, offer one assisted refold; if it remains inaccurate or assembly is unfinished at minute 25, use a prepared paper model. Preserve the learner’s original prediction and let them direct its measurement. Optional scrap hand stitching stops at that deadline too. This recovery is part of the everyday lesson, not just its evaluation.

Learners can predict verbally, point to ruler marks, direct a partner, measure, or record; sewing is unnecessary. Resources are paper templates, rulers, clips, and optional scraps, needles and thread. No donated garments are cut. The mechanism remains comparing equal panels with different seam placement. It assumes straight seams and thin, flat models; finished capacity is outside scope. The added preparation may be worthwhile if it protects reasoning time, but that benefit is untested.
EXPAND.experiment: The facilitator trials this with one small group and records predictions, measured dimensions, completed transfer checks, preparation time, and uses of the fallback. At minute 35, give everyone the same 16 × 14 cm template with 1.5 cm allowances: predict 13 × 12.5 cm before measuring a paper model. Compare completion and explanations with a simple learner-assembled session if available; otherwise treat the first trial as feasibility evidence only. Stop learner assembly at minute 25 regardless of progress. Retain the checkpoint only if it preserves completed prediction checks without the prepared-model handoff obscuring which seam boundaries determine size.

EXPAND.title: Repair a misplaced seam, then verify the repair
EXPAND.proposal:
Upgrade source: “Find why the pouch became narrower.” Preserve diagnosis and repair, but make a failed repair trigger a specific recovery before any stitching. The source’s experiment suggests inspecting failed repairs; this version makes responsibility and recovery explicit in the working lesson.

Prepare two clipped paper models from equal 16 cm-wide panels. The reference has 1 cm side allowances; the other has 1 cm and 3 cm allowances. Keep their bottom allowances equal and tops open. Spend 5 minutes introducing the problem, 7 recording predictions, 10 measuring and diagnosing, 10 repairing and verifying, and 8 explaining and transferring. Expected widths are 14 cm and 12 cm.

Learners identify the misplaced boundary and direct its move from 3 cm to 1 cm. Before changing it, record the expected recovery of 2 cm. The facilitator owns verification: the repaired model must measure within 2 mm of the 14 cm reference. If it fails, check panel alignment and measurement endpoints, then allow one refold. If still unsuccessful by minute 32, the facilitator demonstrates the repair on an already marked spare paper pair while the learner explains the intended change and directs measurement. If a partner leaves or handling becomes difficult, the facilitator takes over manipulation while preserving the learner’s prediction and diagnosis. Optional scrap stitching follows verification only if time remains.

This makes repair success observable and prevents construction error from appearing to disprove correct size reasoning. Paper, rulers, clips and optional scrap sewing tools suffice; no donated garments are cut. Learners may participate entirely through speech, pointing or recording. Straight, flat, unhemmed construction is assumed; the exercise does not teach alteration of an already sewn pouch.
EXPAND.experiment: In one facilitator-led trial, record initial prediction, identified faulty boundary, predicted width recovery, measured repair, assistance time and completed transfer checks. Stop repair attempts at minute 32 and use the demonstration fallback. For transfer, predict and then measure a 16 cm model with 2 cm and 3 cm allowances: its width is 11 cm. Compare with the source procedure on whether learners explain both allowances and finish the check, alongside the extra verification time and facilitator handling. If verification displaces transfer without resolving misleading repair failures, remove the added repair cycle and use a facilitator demonstration immediately after diagnosis.

EXPAND.title: Find the seam that a fold removes
EXPAND.proposal:
Use construction choice as the causal lever: a folded bottom removes one seam allowance deduction. This tests whether learners count the actual seams instead of applying a memorized rule to every pouch.

The facilitator prepares two paper prototypes with equal 16 × 14 cm panel footprints. Model A uses two separate panels, with 1 cm side and bottom allowances. Model B uses one 16 × 28 cm paper piece folded in half to make the same footprint, with 1 cm side allowances and a folded bottom. Both have open, unhemmed tops. Existing paper templates and clips suffice; matching scrap examples are optional, and no donated garments are cut.

Spend 5 minutes identifying joined edges and folded edges, 7 predicting each model’s width and height, 10 clipping and inspecting, 10 measuring and comparing, and 8 on transfer. Before revealing measurements, learners predict which model will be taller and by how much. Model A should measure 14 × 13 cm between its seam boundaries and open top; Model B should measure 14 × 14 cm from its bottom fold to the top. Trace the bottom boundary on each to explain the difference.

The mechanism removes an assumed prerequisite—a sewn bottom—and links size loss to the boundaries actually constructed. The facilitator or a partner can perform every manipulation while learners predict, point, explain or record. Preparation requires accurate paper dimensions and a true midpoint fold. If the footprints do not align within 2 mm, the facilitator refolds once, then uses the marked flat templates to complete the measured comparison. Stop assembly at minute 22. This establishes flat geometry, not fabric capacity; thicker fabric and a top hem would add complications.
EXPAND.experiment: The facilitator runs one 40-minute trial, recording predictions before measurement and explanations afterward. For an unfamiliar transfer case, use 18 × 15 cm panel footprints with 2 cm side allowances: ask learners to predict a folded-bottom model and a model with a 2 cm bottom seam before measuring them. Expected dimensions are 14 × 15 cm and 14 × 13 cm. Compare with the simple same-template lesson on recognizing when height loses an allowance, while recording confusion about the doubled paper length and additional preparation time. Stop introducing construction variants if learners cannot identify the fold versus seam by minute 22; complete the original comparison with facilitator handling. Retain this route only if the construction distinction helps reasoning enough to justify its extra representation demands; superiority is untested.
